titre: The Terracotta Army of Xi'an, Discovered by Farmers (1974)
accroche: In March 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an strike a life-size clay head, and unearth an army buried for 2,200 years.
contenu_vulgarise:
In March 1974, in Lintong County near Xi'an, six brothers of the Yang family and their neighbor Wang Puzhi dig a well on land that has gone barren. As he digs, Yang Zhifa's shovel hits a layer of charcoal and reddened earth; a little deeper, he unearths a human-size clay head. The villagers, convinced they have found a “pottery god,” alert the authorities. What archaeologists uncover in the following months is an army buried for more than 2,000 years to guard the tomb of China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang: to date, more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots, and several hundred horses, spread over three pits.

## Standardized production, 2,000 years before the assembly line

The most striking thing is not the number, it is the method. The imperial workshops did not sculpt each soldier from start to finish: they made heads, arms, legs, and torsos separately from a limited number of molds, then assembled these pieces before customizing each face by hand, mustache, hairstyle, expression. The result gives the illusion of 8,000 unique individuals, whereas production rests on interchangeable components. Another trace of this organization: craftsmen had to inscribe their names on the pieces they produced, a form of quality control that today allows historians to identify distinct workshops, some run by the state, others local.

## What the public has never seen

The soldiers visitors see today are a uniform gray, and that is an optical illusion of history: they came out of the ground painted in bright colors (cinnabar red, malachite green, azurite blue, charcoal black) fixed by a lacquer-based varnish. This varnish cannot withstand Xi'an's dry air: it begins to crack 15 seconds after excavation and flakes off entirely within four minutes, taking the color with it. In other words, a good part of what the excavators of 1974 and the following years saw in color disappeared before it could be preserved. It was this discovery, made at their expense, that led Chinese archaeologists to deliberately slow the excavations: several areas of the site, including a good part of the tomb itself, remain knowingly unexplored today, awaiting conservation techniques able to fix the color before it fades.

repere.texte: The varnish that protected the soldiers' original paint begins to crack 15 seconds after excavation, and flakes off entirely within four minutes: the original cinnabar red, malachite green, and azurite blue have disappeared from most of the figures before they could even be durably photographed.

carte.punch: More than 8,000 soldiers that all seem unique, assembled from standardized parts.
carte.idee: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an discover Emperor Qin's terracotta army: more than 8,000 soldiers, assembled from standardized parts and then customized face by face. Originally painted, they lose their color within minutes in the open air.

quiz.question: How did Emperor Qin's workshops produce 8,000 soldiers that are all different?
choix: By sculpting each soldier by hand, with no interchangeable parts
By assembling standardized parts, then sculpting a distinct face for each one
By casting all the soldiers in a single mold, reused 8,000 times
By hiring 8,000 sculptors, one per soldier, with no common step
quiz.explication: The workshops produced heads, arms, legs, and torsos separately before assembly, and inscribed their names on the pieces for quality control, hence faces that are all different on standardized bodies, and not an individual sculpture or a single mold.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who discovered the Terracotta Army of Xi'an, and under what circumstances?
choix: Archaeologists carrying out a planned excavation in the Xi'an region
Railway workers laying track near Lintong
Chinese soldiers on military maneuvers in Lintong County
Farmers digging a well on land that had gone barren
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Six brothers of the Yang family and their neighbor Wang Puzhi were digging a well on barren land in March 1974 when their shovel hit a clay head, which led to the discovery.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why have the soldiers' original colors almost all disappeared?
choix: Because archaeologists sandblasted them clean before display
Because the original clay held no pigment
Because the protective varnish cracks and flakes off within minutes in the open air
Because the farmers repainted the statues before alerting the authorities
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The lacquer-based varnish that fixed the colors begins to crack 15 seconds after excavation and flakes off entirely within four minutes, taking the color with it.
